sections.title: 11.1 Secure Implementation (Overview)
sections.summary: A control matrix that pairs each attack of module C10 with a control and a live test, and what such tests cannot show.

blocks.markdown:
Defence engineering turns the attack surface of C10 into **controls**, and a control only counts if it has a **test**. NIST SP 800-227 collects the requirements for implementing KEMs in a few headings that this module follows: **input checking** (even benign faults such as accepting an input that is too long or too short can have serious consequences), **failure handling** (a failed operation must not leak information outside the cryptographic module), **side-channel protection** (constant-time implementations, protected memory), **destruction of cryptographic data** as soon as it is no longer needed, and **correct handling of randomness**. FIPS 203 adds that the algorithm's internal functions must not be exposed and that randomness must be generated inside the module (FIPS 203, section 3.3). These requirements are not an implementation guide; the standards say conformance does not by itself guarantee security.

The listing builds a **control matrix** for the ML-KEM reference module of the lab: eight threats from C10, the control that answers each, and a **live test** that runs now and prints PASS or FAIL. The table is the model for every review: no row without a test, and every limitation written down. Everything here runs on your own machine against code and keys that exist only inside the lesson. Where a physical effect is involved (power leakage, injected faults) it is SIMULATED and labelled so. The reference libraries are slow pure-Python code: the lessons show how controls are built and, above all, how to test them.

blocks.markdown:
All eight controls pass their tests in the reference module: truncated and out-of-range inputs are refused, an invalid ciphertext gives the standard's pseudo-random key without an error, every invalid ciphertext produces the same output shape (no visible failure), comparisons of secrets use a constant-time function, an integrity tag detects a corrupted stored key, a key buffer can be wiped, and randomness comes from inside the module. What the matrix deliberately does **not** claim is as important: timing and cache behaviour of *compiled* code, power and fault behaviour of the hardware, the quality of the entropy source and the integrity of the build cannot be shown by tests of this kind; the following lessons give each its own method. **A control that has no test is an assumption.**

**How to use it.** Start every project with the matrix; add a row for each new threat (a new protocol, a new device); write the test before the control; and keep the "not covered" list visible in the review, because that list is the residual risk.

sections.title: 11.2 Constant-Time Design
sections.summary: Branch-free building blocks verified exhaustively, and a bytecode-level tracer that checks that control flow does not depend on the secret, including a blind spot of the simpler line-level tracer.

blocks.markdown:
**Constant-time design** means that the sequence of instructions executed, the memory addresses accessed and the operands of variable-latency instructions do not depend on secret data. The usual rules are no secret-dependent branches, no secret-dependent table indices, no secret operands for division or variable shifts, and comparisons that always process every byte. The standard building blocks are **masks** instead of branches: `ct_select(bit, a, b)` computes (a AND mask) OR (b AND NOT mask) with mask = −bit; a conditional subtraction computes t = x − q and adds q back using the sign of t as a mask; a comparison accumulates the OR of the XORs of all bytes and tests the result once at the end.

Writing such code is half the job; **checking** it is the other half. A practical technique at the source level is to run the function on different secret values and **compare the traces of what executes**; at the binary level the same idea appears as dudect-style statistical timing tests and secret-tainting under a memory checker (11.10). The listing implements the branch-free helpers, verifies each exhaustively against its specification, and then builds two tracers for Python code: one records source lines, the finer one records every bytecode instruction. It uses them on four functions and shows what each tracer can and cannot see. Python is not itself constant time, so this is an exercise in structure and method, not a certification of anything. Everything here runs on your own machine against code and keys that exist only inside the lesson. Where a physical effect is involved (power leakage, injected faults) it is SIMULATED and labelled so. The reference libraries are slow pure-Python code: the lessons show how controls are built and, above all, how to test them.

blocks.markdown:
The helpers match their specifications for 70,000 values of `ct_is_zero`, both bits of select and swap, and all 6,658 inputs of [0, 2q) for the conditional subtraction. The traces separate the functions as intended: the early-exit comparison produces five different traces for six inputs (the work depends on how much of the guess matched), and the `if` version of the conditional subtraction two; the accumulate-and-test comparison and the mask-only subtraction each produce one trace at both levels. The interesting row is the "branch-free" version that still contains a **ternary expression** on one line: the **line-level tracer reports it as constant**, because the whole expression is a single source line, while the **opcode-level tracer reports two different traces**. A tool with a blind spot gives false assurance, so a reviewer must know the resolution of the tool used and prefer the finer one.

**Limits.** The bytecode view still says nothing about the timing of individual instructions, cache behaviour or what a compiler or CPU does with the code. For C and Rust code the equivalent checks run on the compiled binary: statistical timing tests over many secrets, secret-taint tracking, and inspection of the assembly for branches the compiler introduced. **Common mistakes:** trusting a compiler to preserve constant-time source, using comparison operators on secrets, and optimising a "slow" masked helper back into a branch.

sections.title: 11.3 Secure Randomness
sections.summary: An HMAC_DRBG written from SP 800-90A with its properties tested, and continuous health tests that detect a stuck or biased noise source.

blocks.markdown:
FIPS 203, 204 and 205 all require their random inputs to come from an **approved random bit generator (RBG)** built as in the SP 800-90 series: a **noise source** (SP 800-90B) feeds an entropy source whose output seeds a **deterministic random bit generator (DRBG)** (SP 800-90A) that expands it into as many random bytes as needed, reseeding periodically. HMAC_DRBG is one of the approved constructions. It keeps a key K and a value V; the update function mixes new data into both, and generation repeatedly computes V = HMAC(K, V) and outputs V, then updates the state (SP 800-90A Rev. 1, section 10.1.2: instantiate with seed_material = entropy_input ‖ nonce ‖ personalization string, K = 0x00…00, V = 0x01…01, update, and a reseed counter with a reseed interval of 10,000 requests for SHA-256 and a request limit of 7,500 bits).

The listing implements HMAC_DRBG from the algorithm in the standard and tests the properties any correct implementation must have: determinism, sensitivity to every input (entropy, nonce, personalization), advancing state, effect of reseeding, and the request-size limit. Then it implements two **continuous health tests** in the spirit of SP 800-90B, a repetition count test and an adaptive proportion test, and applies them to a healthy source, a source stuck at one value and a biased source. Everything here runs on your own machine against code and keys that exist only inside the lesson. Where a physical effect is involved (power leakage, injected faults) it is SIMULATED and labelled so. The reference libraries are slow pure-Python code: the lessons show how controls are built and, above all, how to test them.

import hashlib, hmac, math, os, random

# --- HMAC_DRBG with SHA-256, written from NIST SP 800-90A Rev. 1, section 10.1.2 (instantiate, update, generate)
class HmacDrbg:
    OUTLEN = 32
    RESEED_INTERVAL = 10_000
    MAX_BYTES_PER_REQUEST = 7500 // 8
    def _hmac(self, key, data):
        return hmac.new(key, data, hashlib.sha256).digest()
    def _update(self, provided_data=b""):
        self.K = self._hmac(self.K, self.V + b"\x00" + provided_data)                # step 1
        self.V = self._hmac(self.K, self.V)                                          # step 2
        if not provided_data:
            return                                                                   # step 3
        self.K = self._hmac(self.K, self.V + b"\x01" + provided_data)                # step 4
        self.V = self._hmac(self.K, self.V)                                          # step 5
    def __init__(self, entropy_input, nonce, personalization=b""):
        seed_material = entropy_input + nonce + personalization
        self.K = b"\x00" * self.OUTLEN
        self.V = b"\x01" * self.OUTLEN
        self._update(seed_material)
        self.reseed_counter = 1
    def reseed(self, entropy_input, additional=b""):
        self._update(entropy_input + additional)
        self.reseed_counter = 1
    def generate(self, n_bytes, additional=b""):
        if n_bytes > self.MAX_BYTES_PER_REQUEST:
            raise ValueError("request too large")
        if self.reseed_counter > self.RESEED_INTERVAL:
            raise RuntimeError("reseed required")
        if additional:
            self._update(additional)
        temp = b""
        while len(temp) < n_bytes:
            self.V = self._hmac(self.K, self.V)
            temp += self.V
        self._update(additional)
        self.reseed_counter += 1
        return temp[:n_bytes]

# properties that must hold for any implementation of the specification
entropy, nonce = hashlib.sha256(b"entropy input for the lesson").digest() + bytes(16), b"nonce-16-bytes!!"
a, b = HmacDrbg(entropy, nonce, b"app"), HmacDrbg(entropy, nonce, b"app")
print("same seed material gives the same output (deterministic):", a.generate(32) == b.generate(32))
print("different personalization string gives different output:", HmacDrbg(entropy, nonce, b"app").generate(32) != HmacDrbg(entropy, nonce, b"other").generate(32))
print("different entropy gives different output:", HmacDrbg(entropy[:-1] + b"X", nonce).generate(32) != HmacDrbg(entropy, nonce).generate(32))
drbg = HmacDrbg(entropy, nonce)
first, second = drbg.generate(32), drbg.generate(32)
print("consecutive outputs differ and the counter advances:", first != second, drbg.reseed_counter == 3)
twin_a, twin_b = HmacDrbg(entropy, nonce), HmacDrbg(entropy, nonce)
twin_b.reseed(b"fresh entropy obtained later")
print("reseeding changes the future output stream (two identical generators diverge after one is reseeded):", twin_a.generate(32) != twin_b.generate(32))
try:
    HmacDrbg(entropy, nonce).generate(938)
    print("a request of 938 bytes was accepted")
except ValueError:
    print("a single request above 7500 bits (937 bytes) is refused, as in the standard's maximum request size")
print("no published known-answer vector is available to this lesson; before use, compare with the NIST CAVP vectors for HMAC_DRBG")

# --- continuous health tests on a noise source, in the spirit of SP 800-90B (repetition count test and adaptive proportion test)
def repetition_count_test(samples, cutoff):
    run, last = 1, None
    for s in samples:
        run = run + 1 if s == last else 1
        last = s
        if run >= cutoff:
            return False
    return True
def adaptive_proportion_test(samples, window, cutoff):
    for start in range(0, len(samples) - window + 1, window):
        block = samples[start:start + window]
        if block.count(block[0]) >= cutoff:
            return False
    return True
rng = random.Random(3)
good = [rng.randrange(256) for _ in range(20000)]                                    # a healthy byte source
stuck = good[:5000] + [77] * 200 + good[5200:]                                       # source that sticks for 200 samples
biased = [0 if rng.random() < 0.4 else rng.randrange(256) for _ in range(20000)]     # one value far too frequent
alpha_cut_rct = 1 + math.ceil(20 / 8)                                                # cutoff for 8 bits of entropy per sample at false-positive rate 2^-20 (RCT: 1 + 20/H)
print()
print(f"{'source':<26} {'repetition count test':>22} {'adaptive proportion test':>26}")
for name, src in (("healthy", good), ("stuck at one value", stuck), ("biased towards 0", biased)):
    print(f"{name:<26} {'pass' if repetition_count_test(src, alpha_cut_rct + 2) else 'FAIL':>22} {'pass' if adaptive_proportion_test(src, 512, 13) else 'FAIL':>26}")
print("the thresholds follow the shape of SP 800-90B (cutoffs derived from the claimed entropy per sample and a false-positive rate); the values here were chosen for the lesson, not copied from the standard")
print("health tests detect a failed source; they do not prove that a source has the entropy claimed. That needs an entropy assessment of the design (SP 800-90B) and a validated generator")

The DRBG behaves as the specification requires: identical seed material gives identical output, a different entropy input or personalization string gives different output, consecutive outputs differ while the reseed counter advances, a reseed makes two otherwise identical generators diverge, and a single request above the limit is refused. The honest limitation is stated in the output: **no published known-answer vector is available in this lesson**, so the implementation is verified against the algorithm's properties and not against the standard's own test vectors, and must be compared with the NIST CAVP vectors before any use. The health tests flag the stuck and the biased sources and pass the healthy one; their cutoffs were chosen for the lesson and not copied from SP 800-90B.

**What the pieces mean.** A DRBG is only as unpredictable as its seed, so the real security lies in the entropy source and its assessment; health tests detect a *failed* source (a stuck sensor, a stuck line), they do not prove that a source has the entropy claimed, and a deterministic generator cannot create entropy it was not given. **Practice:** use the operating system's validated generator, reseed after fork or snapshot restore (10.7), run the start-up and continuous tests of the source in products that carry their own, and never let a caller inject randomness.

sections.title: 11.4 Key Protection
sections.summary: Envelope encryption with authenticated headers, rotation, and threshold secret sharing of a seed, each tested against tampering and against too few custodians.

blocks.markdown:
Keys need protection at rest, in use and during recovery. The standard pattern for **keys at rest** is **envelope encryption**: the private key is stored only after being encrypted ("wrapped") under a **key-encryption key (KEK)** that lives somewhere else, ideally in a hardware security module or a key-management service. The wrapping must be **authenticated** (an AEAD such as AES-GCM), and the **header** that says which algorithm, version and key identifier the blob belongs to must be bound to the ciphertext as associated data, so that an attacker cannot swap labels (an ML-KEM key presented as ML-KEM-512, an old key identifier). **Rotation** replaces the KEK without exposing or changing the wrapped key. For **recovery**, a seed can be split among several custodians with **threshold secret sharing** (Shamir): any t shares reconstruct the secret and fewer than t reveal nothing.

SP 800-227 adds the lifecycle point: cryptographic data must be destroyed as soon as it is no longer needed, including intermediate values and the randomness generated for an encapsulation. The listing wraps an ML-KEM-768 decapsulation key with AES-256-GCM under a header-bound derived key, tests tampering of blob, header and KEK, rotates the KEK, and splits a 64-byte seed 3-of-5 over a prime field, showing that any three shares work and that two shares are consistent with every possible secret. Everything here runs on your own machine against code and keys that exist only inside the lesson. Where a physical effect is involved (power leakage, injected faults) it is SIMULATED and labelled so. The reference libraries are slow pure-Python code: the lessons show how controls are built and, above all, how to test them.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, os, random
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidTag
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF
from kyber_py.ml_kem import ML_KEM_768

# --- envelope encryption: the decapsulation key is stored only wrapped under a key-encryption key (KEK); the header is authenticated, not secret
kem = ML_KEM_768
ek, dk = kem.keygen()
kek = os.urandom(32)                                                       # in practice held by an HSM or key-management service, never stored beside the data
def wrap(kek, key_id, algorithm, secret, version=1):
    header = f"v{version}|{algorithm}|{key_id}".encode()
    nonce = os.urandom(12)
    data_key = HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=32, salt=None, info=b"dk-wrap|" + header).derive(kek)       # a different derived key per header
    return header, nonce, AESGCM(data_key).encrypt(nonce, secret, header)
def unwrap(kek, header, nonce, blob):
    data_key = HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=32, salt=None, info=b"dk-wrap|" + header).derive(kek)
    return AESGCM(data_key).decrypt(nonce, blob, header)
header, nonce, blob = wrap(kek, "key-2026-10-a", "ML-KEM-768", dk)
print("wrapped key blob:", len(blob), "bytes for a", len(dk), "byte key (+16 byte tag); header", header.decode())
print("unwrap restores the key:", unwrap(kek, header, nonce, blob) == dk)
def fails(fn):
    try:
        fn(); return False
    except InvalidTag:
        return True
damaged = bytearray(blob); damaged[100] ^= 1
print("a flipped bit in the blob is detected:", fails(lambda: unwrap(kek, header, nonce, bytes(damaged))))
print("a changed header (algorithm confusion, key-id swap) is detected:", fails(lambda: unwrap(kek, header.replace(b"ML-KEM-768", b"ML-KEM-512"), nonce, blob)))
print("a wrong KEK is detected:", fails(lambda: unwrap(os.urandom(32), header, nonce, blob)))
new_kek = os.urandom(32)
rewrapped = wrap(new_kek, "key-2026-10-b", "ML-KEM-768", unwrap(kek, header, nonce, blob))
print("rotation: unwrap with the old KEK, re-wrap under a new one, and the key itself is unchanged:", unwrap(new_kek, *rewrapped) == dk, "| the old KEK no longer opens the new blob:", fails(lambda: unwrap(kek, *rewrapped)))

# --- splitting the seed among custodians with Shamir secret sharing over a prime field (3 of 5)
P = 2 ** 521 - 1                                                          # a Mersenne prime larger than any 64-byte secret
def split(secret_int, threshold, shares, rng):
    coeffs = [secret_int] + [rng.randrange(P) for _ in range(threshold - 1)]
    return [(x, sum(c * pow(x, i, P) for i, c in enumerate(coeffs)) % P) for x in range(1, shares + 1)]
def combine(points):
    total = 0
    for i, (xi, yi) in enumerate(points):
        num = den = 1
        for j, (xj, _) in enumerate(points):
            if i != j:
                num = num * (-xj) % P
                den = den * (xi - xj) % P
        total = (total + yi * num * pow(den, -1, P)) % P
    return total
rng = random.Random(14)
seed = hashlib.shake_256(b"the 64-byte ML-KEM seed of the lesson").digest(64)
shares = split(int.from_bytes(seed, "big"), 3, 5, rng)
print()
print("any 3 of the 5 shares reconstruct the seed:", all(combine(list(c)).to_bytes(64, "big") == seed for c in __import__("itertools").combinations(shares, 3)))
two = shares[:2]
wrong_candidates = [combine(two + [(3, rng.randrange(P))]) for _ in range(3)]
print("2 shares plus an arbitrary third point give different 'secrets' each time (2 shares fix nothing):", len(set(wrong_candidates)) == 3 and all(c.to_bytes(66, "big")[2:] != seed for c in wrong_candidates))
def poly_through(two_shares, candidate_secret):
    # solve for a1, a2 in  y = candidate + a1 x + a2 x^2  through the two known shares (x = 1 and x = 2)
    (x1, y1), (x2, y2) = two_shares
    det = (x1 * x2 * x2 - x2 * x1 * x1) % P
    r1, r2 = (y1 - candidate_secret) % P, (y2 - candidate_secret) % P
    a1 = (r1 * x2 * x2 - r2 * x1 * x1) * pow(det, -1, P) % P
    a2 = (x1 * r2 - x2 * r1) * pow(det, -1, P) % P
    return a1, a2
def check(two_shares, candidate_secret):
    a1, a2 = poly_through(two_shares, candidate_secret)
    return all((candidate_secret + a1 * x + a2 * x * x) % P == y for x, y in two_shares)
print("for ANY candidate secret there is a degree-2 polynomial through the two known shares, so two shares are consistent with every possible seed:", all(check(two, c) for c in (0, 1, 12345, int.from_bytes(seed, "big"), P - 1)))

sections.title: 11.5 Side-Channel Resistance
sections.summary: Arithmetic masking of a secret polynomial: correct product from shares, single shares that carry no trace of the secret, simulated leakage correlations, and the second-order attack that brings some back.

blocks.markdown:
Constant-time code removes leaks of timing and addresses. **Power and electromagnetic** leakage depends on the *data* being processed, so the remedy is different: **masking** (secret sharing inside the computation). The secret value is split into shares that sum to the secret, for example s = s1 + s2 (mod q) in **arithmetic masking** with a fresh random s1 for every execution; the device handles only the shares, and linear operations are done on each share separately, so that no single intermediate value depends on the secret. This works well for linear steps such as multiplying a secret polynomial by a public one. The hard parts are the **non-linear** operations (comparison, compression and decompression, hashing), which need dedicated masked gadgets and conversions between arithmetic and Boolean masking; masked implementations of lattice schemes are an active research area and are considerably more expensive than unmasked ones. The order of a masking scheme is the number of shares minus one: order-d masking resists attacks that combine up to d measurement points.

This listing is a **SIMULATION** with a Hamming-weight leakage model on a polynomial of the ML-KEM ring. It shows: the product of the secret with a public polynomial is computed from the shares and equals the unmasked product; the distribution of a single share looks the same for two very different secrets (compared with the sampling noise of drawing the same secret twice); the simulated correlation between leakage and secret for unmasked versus masked handling; and a second-order attack that multiplies the centred leakages of the two shares. Everything here runs on your own machine against code and keys that exist only inside the lesson. Where a physical effect is involved (power leakage, injected faults) it is SIMULATED and labelled so. The reference libraries are slow pure-Python code: the lessons show how controls are built and, above all, how to test them.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

# SIMULATION: arithmetic masking of the secret polynomial of a lattice scheme. The secret s is never handled directly: only two shares s1, s2 with
# s1 + s2 = s (mod q) are, and every linear operation is done share by share. The leakage model is the Hamming weight of 12-bit values plus noise.
q, n = 3329, 256
rng = np.random.default_rng(31)
HW = np.array([bin(i).count("1") for i in range(4096)])

def negacyclic_mul(f, g):
    c = np.convolve(f, g)
    c = np.concatenate((c, np.zeros(2 * n - len(c), dtype=c.dtype)))
    return (c[:n] - c[n:]) % q

s = rng.integers(-2, 3, n) % q                                           # a small secret, as in ML-KEM (coefficients in {-2..2} mod q)
s1 = rng.integers(0, q, n)                                               # fresh uniform mask
s2 = (s - s1) % q
u = rng.integers(0, q, n)                                                # a public ciphertext component

# correctness: the product is computed on the shares, and combined only at the end
direct = negacyclic_mul(s, u)
shared = (negacyclic_mul(s1, u) + negacyclic_mul(s2, u)) % q
print("masked computation gives the same product as the unmasked one:", np.array_equal(direct, shared))

# security of a single share: its distribution does not depend on the secret (test with two very different secrets)
def share_histogram(secret, trials=4000):
    counts = np.zeros(q)
    for _ in range(trials):
        mask = rng.integers(0, q, n)
        counts += np.bincount(mask, minlength=q)            # the first share is the mask itself, uniform by construction
        counts += np.bincount((secret - mask) % q, minlength=q)
    return counts / counts.sum()
zero_secret, big_secret = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.int64), np.full(n, 2, dtype=np.int64)
h0, h0_again, h1 = share_histogram(zero_secret, 300), share_histogram(zero_secret, 300), share_histogram(big_secret, 300)
tv = lambda a, b: 0.5 * np.abs(a - b).sum()
print(f"distance between share distributions: same secret drawn twice {tv(h0, h0_again):.4f} (pure sampling noise); different secrets 'all 0' and 'all 2' {tv(h0, h1):.4f}")
print("the two distances are of the same size: the distribution of a single share carries no visible trace of the secret")

# leakage: correlation between the observed leakage and the true secret coefficient, with and without masking
def correlation(values_handled, secret_values, noise=1.0, traces=60000):
    idx = rng.integers(0, n, traces)
    leakage = HW[values_handled[idx] % 4096] + rng.normal(0, noise, traces)
    return abs(np.corrcoef(leakage, HW[secret_values[idx] % 4096])[0, 1])
secret_small = (s % q)
unmasked = correlation(s, secret_small)
masked_share_1 = correlation(s1, secret_small)
masked_share_2 = correlation(s2, secret_small)
print(f"correlation of the leakage with the secret: unmasked {unmasked:.3f}; handling only share 1 {masked_share_1:.3f}; handling only share 2 {masked_share_2:.3f}")
# a second-order attack combines the leakage of both shares: the product of the centred leakages correlates with the secret
idx = rng.integers(0, n, 200000)
l1 = HW[s1[idx]] + rng.normal(0, 1.0, len(idx))
l2 = HW[s2[idx]] + rng.normal(0, 1.0, len(idx))
combined = (l1 - l1.mean()) * (l2 - l2.mean())
second_order = abs(np.corrcoef(combined, HW[s[idx]])[0, 1])
print(f"second-order attack combining the leakage of both shares: correlation {second_order:.3f}")
print("first-order masking removes the first-order correlation; combining two measurement points can bring a (smaller) correlation back, which is why a stated masking order and its cost matter")
print("the hard parts in a real scheme are the non-linear steps (decompression, comparison, hashing), which need dedicated masked gadgets; the linear arithmetic shown here is the easy case")

The masked computation gives the same product. The distance between the share distributions for two different secrets (0.0850) is of the same size as the distance between two draws for the *same* secret (0.0824), which is pure sampling noise: a single share carries no visible trace of the secret. In the leakage model the correlation with the secret is 0.963 when the secret is handled directly and only 0.017 and 0.047 for handling a single share. The second-order attack, which combines the leakage of both shares, brings a correlation of about 0.18 back: masking has not made the secret safe against an attacker who can observe both share computations, it has raised the cost, because the attacker now needs the two measurement points and many more traces (the cost of such attacks grows with the masking order and the noise).

**Takeaways.** Masking trades speed and area for resistance to a stated order of attack; the claim must name the order, the leakage model and the platform; a masked implementation must itself be tested with leakage-evaluation methods (statistical tests on measured traces) because a mistake in a gadget can leak at first order; and masking combines with hiding (noise, shuffling) and with protocol limits on key use. **Common mistake:** masking the arithmetic but unmasking for the comparison or the hash, which brings the secret back into a single value.

sections.title: 11.6 Fault Detection
sections.summary: Measured detection rates of verify-before-release and recompute-and-compare for 300 injected RSA-CRT faults, ML-DSA output faults, redundant ML-KEM decapsulation, and the faults these checks cannot catch.

blocks.markdown:
10.5 showed that one faulty output can reveal a key. **Fault detection** adds checks so that a faulty result is **never released**. The main techniques are: **verify before release** (a signer verifies its own signature with the public key before output; it costs one verification), **redundancy** (compute twice, or compute the inverse operation, and compare), **integrity checks on keys and constants** (9.4), **control-flow integrity** (so one glitch cannot skip a check), and **hedged randomness** in signatures, which FIPS 204 says makes fault attacks easier to mitigate than the deterministic variant. The weakness of every software check is that it is itself software: an attacker who can skip the comparison, or inject the same fault twice, defeats a naive version.

The listing injects 300 random single-bit faults into the two halves of an RSA-CRT signature and records the outcome of three signers: unprotected, verify-before-release, and recompute-and-compare. It then corrupts 120 finished ML-DSA-44 signatures at random positions behind a signer that verifies its output, and runs redundant ML-KEM decapsulation with a transient fault in one of the two runs. All faults are **SIMULATED in software**. Everything here runs on your own machine against code and keys that exist only inside the lesson. Where a physical effect is involved (power leakage, injected faults) it is SIMULATED and labelled so. The reference libraries are slow pure-Python code: the lessons show how controls are built and, above all, how to test them.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, random
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa
from kyber_py.ml_kem import ML_KEM_768
from dilithium_py.ml_dsa import ML_DSA_44

rng = random.Random(16)
# SIMULATION of single-bit faults injected in software. Detection rate = fraction of injected faults for which a faulty result is NEVER released.

# --- 1. RSA-CRT signing with three protection levels
numbers = rsa.generate_private_key(65537, 1024).private_numbers()
p, q, e = numbers.p, numbers.q, numbers.public_numbers.e
n = p * q
dp, dq, qinv = numbers.dmp1, numbers.dmq1, numbers.iqmp
def crt(m, flip_p=None, flip_q=None):
    sp, sq = pow(m, dp, p), pow(m, dq, q)
    if flip_p is not None: sp ^= 1 << flip_p
    if flip_q is not None: sq ^= 1 << flip_q
    return sq + (qinv * (sp - sq) % p) * q
def unprotected(m, fault):
    return crt(m, *fault)
def verify_then_release(m, fault):
    s = crt(m, *fault)
    return s if pow(s, e, n) == m else None
def redundant_and_compare(m, fault):
    first = crt(m, *fault)
    second = crt(m)                                                       # the second execution is assumed fault-free here; an attacker with two faults could defeat a naive repeat
    return first if first == second else None
trials = 300
stats = {"no countermeasure": 0, "verify before release": 0, "recompute and compare": 0}
leaked_factor = 0
for _ in range(trials):
    m = rng.randrange(2, n)
    fault = (None, rng.randrange(0, 512)) if rng.random() < 0.5 else (rng.randrange(0, 512), None)
    good = pow(m, numbers.d, n)
    out = unprotected(m, fault)
    if out != good:
        stats["no countermeasure"] += 1
        import math
        leaked_factor += math.gcd(pow(out, e, n) - m, n) in (p, q)
    stats["verify before release"] += verify_then_release(m, fault) is None
    stats["recompute and compare"] += redundant_and_compare(m, fault) is None
print(f"{trials} random single-bit faults in the CRT halves:")
print(f"  unprotected signer released a faulty signature {stats['no countermeasure']} times, and {leaked_factor} of them revealed a prime factor of n")
print(f"  verify-before-release withheld {stats['verify before release']} of {trials} faulty results; recompute-and-compare withheld {stats['recompute and compare']} of {trials}")

# --- 2. ML-DSA: the signer verifies its own signature before releasing it (costs one verification)
dsa = ML_DSA_44
pk, sk = dsa.keygen()
def sign_protected(message, fault_position=None):
    sig = bytearray(dsa.sign(sk, message))
    if fault_position is not None:
        sig[fault_position] ^= 1 << rng.randrange(8)                       # a fault that corrupts the finished signature
    sig = bytes(sig)
    return sig if dsa.verify(pk, message, sig) else None
released_bad = withheld = 0
for _ in range(120):
    msg = bytes(rng.getrandbits(8) for _ in range(20))
    out = sign_protected(msg, rng.randrange(2420))
    withheld += out is None
    released_bad += out is not None and not dsa.verify(pk, msg, out)
print(f"ML-DSA-44, 120 faults in the output signature: withheld {withheld}, faulty signatures released {released_bad}")
print("faults that occur in the signing computation BEFORE the signature is formed usually produce signatures that fail verification, and the same check catches them")
print("what the check cannot catch: a fault that skips the verification itself (use redundancy and control-flow integrity), and faults in the private key before it is used (a faulty key is a different key and signs 'validly')")

# --- 3. ML-KEM: decapsulating twice and comparing detects transient faults; permanent faults need the key integrity checks of 9.4
kem = ML_KEM_768
ek, dk = kem.keygen()
key, ct = kem.encaps(ek)
def decaps_redundant(dk_bytes, c, fault=None):
    first = kem.decaps(dk_bytes if fault is None else dk_bytes, c)
    if fault is not None:
        first = bytes(b ^ (1 << fault) if i == 0 else b for i, b in enumerate(first))      # transient fault corrupts the first result only
    second = kem.decaps(dk_bytes, c)
    return first if first == second else None
print("ML-KEM redundant decapsulation: no fault ->", decaps_redundant(dk, ct) == key, "| transient fault in one run -> result withheld:", decaps_redundant(dk, ct, fault=3) is None)

The unprotected signer released a faulty signature in all 300 cases and **every one of them revealed a prime factor** of the modulus. Verify-before-release and recompute-and-compare each withheld all 300 faulty results. The ML-DSA signer that verifies its output withheld all 120 corrupted signatures and released no faulty one, and redundant ML-KEM decapsulation withheld the result when one of the two runs was disturbed, while passing the fault-free case. **Design guidance.** Choose the check by what it costs and what it covers: verification is cheap for RSA and expensive for ML-DSA (about the cost of a verification, ~10 ms in the pure-Python reference of 9.10); redundancy doubles the work; hardware fault sensors and shielding address the physical side. Combine checks so that no single glitch can both cause the fault and skip the check, and test the checks with a fault-injection campaign as the lesson does, reporting the detection rate and the cases not covered.

sections.title: 11.7 Secure APIs
sections.summary: A public-key encryption format built from a KEM, a standard AEAD and a strict versioned header, attacked with algorithm confusion, replay across contexts, version tampering and truncation.

blocks.markdown:
9.8 gave the rules for a hard-to-misuse API; this lesson applies them to a **message format**. A KEM does not encrypt data. The standard construction (SP 800-227 describes KEMs as the basis for KEM/DEM public-key encryption) uses the KEM to agree a key and a standard **AEAD** to encrypt the data with it, and the details that make it secure are in the format: the header names the algorithms and the version; the derived key is **bound to the header and the KEM ciphertext** so that nothing can be changed without breaking decryption; a **context string** ties a message to its purpose; parsing is **strict** (exact lengths, known identifiers, matching key type) and all failures produce the **same error**, raised before any secret-dependent processing where possible.

The listing implements the format "magic | version | KEM id | AEAD id | context length | context | KEM ciphertext | nonce | AEAD ciphertext" with ML-KEM-768 or ML-KEM-1024 selected by an identifier and AES-256-GCM, and then attacks it: wrong expected context, a header that names another KEM (algorithm confusion), an unknown version, flipped bits in each part, truncation and the wrong recipient key. Everything here runs on your own machine against code and keys that exist only inside the lesson. Where a physical effect is involved (power leakage, injected faults) it is SIMULATED and labelled so. The reference libraries are slow pure-Python code: the lessons show how controls are built and, above all, how to test them.

blocks.code:
import os, struct
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidTag
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import mlkem, mldsa
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF

# A public-key encryption format built the safe way: a KEM produces a key, a standard AEAD encrypts, and a strict, versioned header is authenticated.
# Format: magic(4) | version(1) | kem_id(1) | aead_id(1) | context_len(1) | context | kem_ciphertext | nonce(12) | aead_ciphertext
MAGIC = b"QSEA"
KEM_IDS = {1: ("ML-KEM-768", mlkem.MLKEM768PrivateKey, mlkem.MLKEM768PublicKey, 1088), 2: ("ML-KEM-1024", mlkem.MLKEM1024PrivateKey, mlkem.MLKEM1024PublicKey, 1568)}
AEAD_IDS = {1: "AES-256-GCM"}
ACCEPTED_VERSIONS = {1}

def seal(public_key, kem_id, plaintext, context=b""):
    name, priv_cls, pub_cls, ct_len = KEM_IDS[kem_id]
    shared, kem_ct = public_key.encapsulate()
    header = MAGIC + struct.pack("BBBB", 1, kem_id, 1, len(context)) + context
    key = HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=32, salt=None, info=b"sealed-v1|" + header + kem_ct).derive(shared)        # the key is bound to the header and the KEM ciphertext
    nonce = os.urandom(12)
    return header + kem_ct + nonce + AESGCM(key).encrypt(nonce, plaintext, header + kem_ct)

class FormatError(Exception):
    pass

def open_sealed(private_key, blob, expected_context=b""):
    # strict parsing: every failure is the same FormatError, raised before any decryption
    if len(blob) < 8 or blob[:4] != MAGIC:
        raise FormatError("invalid message")
    version, kem_id, aead_id, ctx_len = struct.unpack("BBBB", blob[4:8])
    if version not in ACCEPTED_VERSIONS or kem_id not in KEM_IDS or aead_id not in AEAD_IDS:
        raise FormatError("invalid message")
    name, priv_cls, pub_cls, ct_len = KEM_IDS[kem_id]
    if not isinstance(private_key, priv_cls):
        raise FormatError("invalid message")                                         # algorithm confusion: the key type must match the declared KEM
    pos = 8
    context = blob[pos:pos + ctx_len]; pos += ctx_len
    if context != expected_context or len(blob) < pos + ct_len + 12 + 16:
        raise FormatError("invalid message")
    header = blob[:pos]
    kem_ct = blob[pos:pos + ct_len]; pos += ct_len
    nonce, body = blob[pos:pos + 12], blob[pos + 12:]
    shared = private_key.decapsulate(kem_ct)
    key = HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=32, salt=None, info=b"sealed-v1|" + header + kem_ct).derive(shared)
    try:
        return AESGCM(key).decrypt(nonce, body, header + kem_ct)
    except InvalidTag:
        raise FormatError("invalid message")

def outcome(fn):
    try:
        return "accepted: " + fn().decode()
    except FormatError as exc:
        return f"FormatError ({exc})"

recipient768 = mlkem.MLKEM768PrivateKey.generate()
recipient1024 = mlkem.MLKEM1024PrivateKey.generate()
blob = seal(recipient768.public_key(), 1, b"quarterly report", context=b"finance")
print("message size", len(blob), "bytes = header 15 + KEM ciphertext 1,088 + nonce 12 + plaintext 16 + tag 16 =", 15 + 1088 + 12 + 16 + 16)
print("honest open:", outcome(lambda: open_sealed(recipient768, blob, b"finance")))
print("wrong expected context (replay in another purpose):", outcome(lambda: open_sealed(recipient768, blob, b"hr")))
tampered_header = bytearray(blob); tampered_header[5] = 2
print("header says ML-KEM-1024 but the key is ML-KEM-768 (algorithm confusion):", outcome(lambda: open_sealed(recipient768, bytes(tampered_header), b"finance")))
unknown_version = bytearray(blob); unknown_version[4] = 9
print("unknown version number:", outcome(lambda: open_sealed(recipient768, bytes(unknown_version), b"finance")))
flipped = bytearray(blob); flipped[-1] ^= 1
print("one bit flipped in the authenticated ciphertext:", outcome(lambda: open_sealed(recipient768, bytes(flipped), b"finance")))
flipped_kem = bytearray(blob); flipped_kem[30] ^= 1
print("one bit flipped in the KEM ciphertext (implicit rejection, then the AEAD fails):", outcome(lambda: open_sealed(recipient768, bytes(flipped_kem), b"finance")))
print("truncated message:", outcome(lambda: open_sealed(recipient768, blob[:-1], b"finance")))
print("wrong recipient key:", outcome(lambda: open_sealed(mlkem.MLKEM768PrivateKey.generate(), blob, b"finance")))
blob2 = seal(recipient1024.public_key(), 2, b"quarterly report", context=b"finance")
print("same format with ML-KEM-1024 selected by the identifier:", outcome(lambda: open_sealed(recipient1024, blob2, b"finance")), "| size", len(blob2))
print("all failures return the same message and happen before or inside authenticated decryption; no variant reveals which check failed")

The honest message opens; the message size is exactly the sum of its parts (15 + 1,088 + 12 + 16 + 16 = 1,147 bytes for a 16-byte plaintext). Every attack ends in the same `FormatError (invalid message)` with no detail: a message sealed for the "finance" context is refused for "hr", a header naming ML-KEM-1024 is refused by an ML-KEM-768 key (algorithm confusion), an unknown version is refused, and flipped bits in the AEAD part or in the KEM ciphertext are refused (for the KEM ciphertext, implicit rejection produces an unrelated key and the AEAD then fails). sections.title: 11.8 Algorithm Agility
sections.summary: A registry-and-policy layer that swaps algorithms by configuration, enforces deprecation dates, and an inventory check that shows where agility does not reach.

blocks.markdown:
**Algorithm agility** is the ability to change cryptographic algorithms without redesigning the system. It matters for two reasons: the migration to post-quantum algorithms is not a one-off event (parameters and algorithms will continue to change as analysis improves, as 8.10 and the NIST status reports show), and a flaw discovered in one algorithm must be removable quickly. Agility has three parts: a **registry** that maps algorithm identifiers to implementations, a **policy** (kept in configuration, versioned and signed) that says which identifiers are allowed, deprecated with a **sunset date**, or forbidden, and **identifiers carried in every key, certificate, ciphertext and signature** so that old and new data can be processed side by side (11.7).

Agility has a cost and a risk. The cost is complexity and more code paths to test; the risk is **downgrade**: a system that supports many algorithms can be pushed to the weakest (10.9), so the policy must remove weak options, not just add new ones. The listing implements the registry and the policy, requests algorithms (default, deprecated, unknown, not allowed), shows a deprecated algorithm being refused after its sunset date, changes the default KEM by editing the policy, and checks an (invented) usage log against the registry to find usage that bypasses it. Everything here runs on your own machine against code and keys that exist only inside the lesson. Where a physical effect is involved (power leakage, injected faults) it is SIMULATED and labelled so. The reference libraries are slow pure-Python code: the lessons show how controls are built and, above all, how to test them.

import datetime, json
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import mlkem, mldsa, ec
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes

# --- algorithm agility through a registry and a policy that lives in configuration, not in code
REGISTRY = {
    "ml-kem-768": {"kind": "kem", "make": mlkem.MLKEM768PrivateKey.generate, "level": 3},
    "ml-kem-1024": {"kind": "kem", "make": mlkem.MLKEM1024PrivateKey.generate, "level": 5},
    "ml-dsa-44": {"kind": "sig", "make": mldsa.MLDSA44PrivateKey.generate, "level": 2},
    "ml-dsa-65": {"kind": "sig", "make": mldsa.MLDSA65PrivateKey.generate, "level": 3},
    "ecdsa-p256": {"kind": "sig", "make": lambda: ec.generate_private_key(ec.SECP256R1()), "level": 1},
}
POLICY_JSON = """
{"version": 7,
 "kem": {"default": "ml-kem-768", "allowed": ["ml-kem-768", "ml-kem-1024"]},
 "sig": {"default": "ml-dsa-65", "allowed": ["ml-dsa-65", "ml-dsa-44", "ecdsa-p256"],
         "deprecated": {"ecdsa-p256": "2027-12-31"}, "forbidden": []}}
"""
policy = json.loads(POLICY_JSON)

def make_key(kind, requested=None, today=datetime.date(2026, 10, 4)):
    name = requested or policy[kind]["default"]
    entry = policy[kind]
    if name not in REGISTRY or REGISTRY[name]["kind"] != kind:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown {kind} algorithm {name!r}")
    if name in entry.get("forbidden", []) or name not in entry["allowed"]:
        raise ValueError(f"{name} is not allowed by policy version {policy['version']}")
    note = ""
    if name in entry.get("deprecated", {}):
        sunset = datetime.date.fromisoformat(entry["deprecated"][name])
        if today > sunset:
            raise ValueError(f"{name} passed its sunset date {sunset}")
        note = f" (deprecated, sunset {sunset}, {(sunset - today).days} days left)"
    return name, REGISTRY[name]["make"](), note

for kind, requested in (("kem", None), ("sig", None), ("sig", "ecdsa-p256"), ("kem", "ml-kem-512"), ("sig", "ml-dsa-87")):
    try:
        name, key, note = make_key(kind, requested)
        print(f"{kind} request {str(requested):<12} -> {name}{note}")
    except ValueError as exc:
        print(f"{kind} request {str(requested):<12} -> refused: {exc}")
later = datetime.date(2028, 1, 15)
try:
    make_key("sig", "ecdsa-p256", today=later)
except ValueError as exc:
    print(f"on {later}: refused: {exc}")

# changing the algorithm is a configuration change: the same application code, a different default
policy["kem"]["default"] = "ml-kem-1024"
policy["version"] = 8
name, key, _ = make_key("kem")
print("after policy version 8 the default KEM is", name, "- no code change, but every stored ciphertext format must carry the algorithm identifier (11.7) so old and new data can both be read")

# an inventory query: which algorithms does the application's own usage log still rely on?
# DEMO DATA: an invented usage log for illustration, not a measurement of any system
usage_log = [("ecdsa-p256", 4120), ("ml-dsa-65", 310), ("ml-kem-768", 2300), ("rsa-2048", 85)]
print()
print("DEMO DATA (invented usage counts):")
print(f"{'algorithm in use':<18} {'operations':>11} {'registered':>11} {'policy status'}")
for name, count in usage_log:

    elif name in policy["sig"].get("deprecated", {}):

    elif name in policy["sig"]["allowed"] + policy["kem"]["allowed"]:
        status = "allowed"
    else:
        status = "not allowed"
    print(f"{name:<18} {count:>11,} {str(registered):>11} {status}")
print("agility is only as real as its coverage: usage that bypasses the registry (here rsa-2048) cannot be migrated by changing the configuration")

sections.title: 11.9 Hybrid Deployment
sections.summary: The X25519MLKEM768 key exchange built to the byte layout of RFC 10024, with sizes, the break-one-component experiment, the failure behaviour of each part, and the operational costs.

blocks.markdown:
Most early deployments use **hybrid** key exchange: a classical and a post-quantum exchange run together and their secrets are combined, so the result stays secure if either holds (10.10 covered the combiner). For TLS the group **X25519MLKEM768** is specified in RFC 10024: the client's key-exchange value is the ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key followed by the X25519 share (1,184 + 32 = 1,216 bytes); the server's is the ML-KEM ciphertext followed by its X25519 share (1,088 + 32 = 1,120 bytes); and the shared secret is the **ML-KEM secret followed by the X25519 secret**, 64 bytes, fed to the protocol's HKDF-based key schedule. Both sides must perform the all-zero check on the X25519 secret and abort if it fails. (The group's name lists X25519 first while the concatenation puts ML-KEM first, for historical reasons the RFC notes; ML-KEM's secret comes first so that a FIPS-validated ML-KEM implementation satisfies the SP 800-56C condition that the first secret comes from an approved scheme.)

The listing implements exactly that byte layout with OpenSSL-backed keys, checks sizes and agreement, and then experiments: it gives the attacker the X25519 secret and then the ML-KEM secret in turn, and shows what a tampered ciphertext and malformed shares do. Everything here runs on your own machine against code and keys that exist only inside the lesson. Where a physical effect is involved (power leakage, injected faults) it is SIMULATED and labelled so. The reference libraries are slow pure-Python code: the lessons show how controls are built and, above all, how to test them.

import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import mlkem
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.x25519 import X25519PrivateKey, X25519PublicKey
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF

raw = lambda pub: pub.public_bytes_raw()

# --- the X25519MLKEM768 key exchange as specified in RFC 10024, sections 4.1 to 4.3 (the byte layout is the point)
def client_share():
    kem_private = mlkem.MLKEM768PrivateKey.generate()
    x_private = X25519PrivateKey.generate()
    share = raw(kem_private.public_key()) + raw(x_private.public_key())              # ML-KEM encapsulation key first, then the X25519 share
    return share, (kem_private, x_private)
def server_respond(share):
    ek, x_peer = share[:1184], share[1184:]
    if len(share) != 1216:
        raise ValueError("bad client share length")
    shared_kem, kem_ct = mlkem.MLKEM768PublicKey.from_public_bytes(ek).encapsulate()
    x_private = X25519PrivateKey.generate()
    shared_x = x_private.exchange(X25519PublicKey.from_public_bytes(x_peer))
    if shared_x == bytes(32):
        raise ValueError("all-zero X25519 shared secret: abort")                       # RFC 10024 section 4.3 requires this check
    return kem_ct + raw(x_private.public_key()), shared_kem + shared_x               # server share, 64-byte shared secret (ML-KEM part first)
def client_finish(server_share, client_state):
    kem_private, x_private = client_state
    if len(server_share) != 1120:
        raise ValueError("bad server share length")
    kem_ct, x_peer = server_share[:1088], server_share[1088:]
    shared_kem = kem_private.decapsulate(kem_ct)
    shared_x = x_private.exchange(X25519PublicKey.from_public_bytes(x_peer))
    if shared_x == bytes(32):
        raise ValueError("all-zero X25519 shared secret: abort")
    return shared_kem + shared_x

share, state = client_share()
server_share, secret_server = server_respond(share)
secret_client = client_finish(server_share, state)
print(f"client share {len(share)} bytes (1,184 ML-KEM + 32 X25519), server share {len(server_share)} bytes (1,088 + 32), shared secret {len(secret_client)} bytes (32 + 32): sizes as in RFC 10024")
print("both sides derive the same 64-byte secret:", secret_client == secret_server)
agree = 0
for _ in range(25):
    sh, st = client_share(); ss, sec_s = server_respond(sh)
    agree += client_finish(ss, st) == sec_s
print("25 further exchanges agree:", agree == 25, "| the two components are independent values:", secret_client[:32] != secret_client[32:])
key_schedule = lambda secret: HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=32, salt=None, info=b"handshake key").derive(secret)
print("the 64-byte secret feeds the protocol's key derivation (HKDF in TLS 1.3):", len(key_schedule(secret_client)), "byte key")

# --- the point of a hybrid: break ONE component and the other still protects the key
def derived_key(kem_part, x_part):
    return key_schedule(kem_part + x_part)
true_key = derived_key(secret_client[:32], secret_client[32:])
print()
print("SIMULATION: attacker learns the X25519 secret (quantum adversary) but must guess the ML-KEM secret:", derived_key(os.urandom(32), secret_client[32:]) == true_key, "(key not recovered)")
print("SIMULATION: attacker learns the ML-KEM secret (a flaw in the new algorithm) but must guess the X25519 secret:", derived_key(secret_client[:32], os.urandom(32)) == true_key, "(key not recovered)")
print("only when BOTH components are known does the attacker obtain the key:", derived_key(secret_client[:32], secret_client[32:]) == true_key)

# --- failure behaviour: what happens if one component fails or is attacked
bad_server = bytearray(server_share); bad_server[7] ^= 1                             # the ML-KEM ciphertext is tampered with
tampered_secret = client_finish(bytes(bad_server), state)
print()
print("tampered ML-KEM ciphertext: no exception, the ML-KEM part changes (implicit rejection) and the X25519 part does not:", tampered_secret[:32] != secret_client[:32], tampered_secret[32:] == secret_client[32:], "-> the handshake fails later at the Finished check")
for length_case, blob in (("truncated client share", share[:-1]), ("empty client share", b"")):
    try:
        server_respond(blob); print(length_case, "accepted")
    except ValueError as exc:
        print(f"{length_case}: refused ({exc})")
try:
    server_respond(share[:1184] + bytes(32))
except ValueError as exc:
    print("client share whose X25519 part is the all-zero (low-order) point: refused, ->", exc)
print("operational costs of the hybrid: the first flight grows by about 1.2 KB each way, the client and server both pay for two key exchanges, and both algorithms must be kept patched")

The sizes are those of the RFC (1,216 and 1,120 bytes, a 64-byte secret), and the two sides agree in all 26 exchanges tried. The break-one-component experiment shows the purpose of the design: an attacker who knows only the X25519 secret (the quantum case) or only the ML-KEM secret (the case of a flaw in the new algorithm) cannot derive the key, and only knowing both does. A tampered ML-KEM ciphertext changes the ML-KEM part (implicit rejection) and not the X25519 part, so the handshake fails later at the Finished check; malformed or truncated shares and the all-zero X25519 point are refused.

The hybrid is a **transition** measure: its removal date should be part of the migration plan.

sections.title: 11.10 Testing
sections.summary: A mutation fuzzer run against ML-KEM and ML-DSA parsers with outcome classification, cross-checked against OpenSSL, and what fuzzing does and does not prove.

blocks.markdown:
Testing a cryptographic component has layers that earlier lessons built one at a time: **known-answer tests** (9.12), **differential testing** against an independent implementation (9.11), **property tests** (round trips, determinism), **negative tests** (invalid inputs), **timing and constant-time tests** (11.2), and **fuzzing**. Fuzzing feeds a program large numbers of automatically mutated inputs and watches for failures: crashes, hangs, memory errors (under sanitizers), and *unexpected* behaviour. For a parser of untrusted bytes the **oracle** is simple to state: the result must be one of a small set of acceptable outcomes: a valid answer or a clean, expected refusal, never an unexpected exception, a hang or an accepted forgery.

The listing implements a small **mutation fuzzer** (bit flips, byte substitution, truncation, extension, splicing, runs of zeros and of 0xFF) and applies it to four parsers: ML-KEM-768 decapsulation (1,500 mutated ciphertexts), ML-KEM encapsulation key parsing (1,500 mutated keys), ML-DSA-44 verification (400 mutated signatures and 200 mutated public keys), and then compares the verdicts of the pure-Python and OpenSSL implementations on 300 mutated signatures. Every outcome is classified, and anything outside the expected set would be reported as UNEXPECTED. Everything here runs on your own machine against code and keys that exist only inside the lesson. Where a physical effect is involved (power leakage, injected faults) it is SIMULATED and labelled so. The reference libraries are slow pure-Python code: the lessons show how controls are built and, above all, how to test them.

blocks.code:
import random
from collections import Counter
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidSignature
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import mlkem, mldsa
from kyber_py.ml_kem import ML_KEM_768
from dilithium_py.ml_dsa import ML_DSA_44

rng = random.Random(1110)

def mutate(data):
    data = bytearray(data)
    kind = rng.choice(("bitflip", "byte", "truncate", "extend", "splice", "zero-run", "ff-run"))
    if kind == "bitflip" and data:
        for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 4)):
            data[rng.randrange(len(data))] ^= 1 << rng.randrange(8)
    elif kind == "byte" and data:
        data[rng.randrange(len(data))] = rng.randrange(256)
    elif kind == "truncate" and data:
        del data[rng.randrange(len(data)):]
    elif kind == "extend":
        data += bytes(rng.getrandbits(8) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 40)))
    elif kind == "splice" and len(data) > 8:
        i, j = rng.randrange(len(data)), rng.randrange(len(data))
        data[i:i + 4] = data[j:j + 4]
    elif kind == "zero-run" and data:
        i = rng.randrange(len(data)); data[i:i + rng.randint(1, 64)] = bytes(min(64, len(data) - i))
    elif kind == "ff-run" and data:
        i = rng.randrange(len(data)); n = min(rng.randint(1, 64), len(data) - i); data[i:i + n] = b"\xff" * n
    return bytes(data), kind

def classify(fn):
    try:
        result = fn()
        return "returned"
    except (ValueError, InvalidSignature):
        return "refused (expected error type)"
    except Exception as exc:
        return "UNEXPECTED " + type(exc).__name__

# --- ML-KEM decapsulation: every mutated ciphertext must either be refused for length or yield SOME 32-byte key (implicit rejection); never anything else
kem = ML_KEM_768
ek, dk = kem.key_derive(bytes(range(64)))                                   # fixed keys and message keep the run reproducible
key, ct = kem._encaps_internal(ek, bytes(32))
outcomes, lengths_ok = Counter(), Counter()
for _ in range(1500):
    bad, kind = mutate(ct)
    got = []
    outcome = classify(lambda: got.append(kem.decaps(dk, bad)))
    outcomes[outcome] += 1
    if got:
        lengths_ok[(len(bad) == len(ct), len(got[0]) == 32, got[0] == key)] += 1
print("ML-KEM-768 decaps, 1,500 mutated ciphertexts:", dict(outcomes))
print("  among those that returned a key: (correct length, 32-byte key, equals the honest key):", dict(lengths_ok))

# --- ML-KEM encapsulation-key parsing, mutated public keys
outcomes = Counter()
for _ in range(1500):
    bad, kind = mutate(ek)
    outcomes[classify(lambda: kem.encaps(bad))] += 1
print("ML-KEM-768 encaps on 1,500 mutated public keys:", dict(outcomes))

# --- ML-DSA verification with mutated signatures, messages and keys: the verdict must be a boolean or a clean refusal
dsa = ML_DSA_44
pk, sk = dsa.key_derive(bytes(32))
msg = b"fuzz target message"
sig = dsa.sign(sk, msg, deterministic=True)
verdicts = Counter()
for _ in range(400):
    bad, kind = mutate(sig)
    box = []
    out = classify(lambda: box.append(dsa.verify(pk, msg, bad)))
    verdicts[out if not box else ("accepted" if box[0] else "rejected")] += 1
print("ML-DSA-44 verify on 400 mutated signatures:", dict(verdicts))
verdicts = Counter()
for _ in range(200):
    bad, kind = mutate(pk)
    box = []
    out = classify(lambda: box.append(dsa.verify(bad, msg, sig)))
    verdicts[out if not box else ("accepted" if box[0] else "rejected")] += 1
print("ML-DSA-44 verify under 200 mutated public keys:", dict(verdicts))

# --- the independent implementation under the same mutated inputs: do both libraries give the same verdict?

    py_verdict = dsa.verify(pk0, msg, bad)
    same += py_verdict == ssl_verdict
    total += 1

sections.title: 11.11 Formal-Verification Concepts
sections.summary: Verification by exhaustion of Montgomery and Barrett reduction over their whole input ranges, and an explicit-state model check of the downgrade scenario, with a clear statement of what each proves.

blocks.markdown:
**Formal verification** replaces "we tested it" with a proof that holds for *all* inputs within a stated model. It comes in several strengths. The most accessible is **verification by exhaustion**: when the input domain is small enough, check every input; the result is a complete proof for that domain and it fails loudly if a constant is wrong. At the other end, **proof assistants and verified toolchains** (machine-checked proofs of functional correctness, of constant-time behaviour and of security reductions, for example with Coq, EasyCrypt, Jasmin or Cryptol/SAW-style tools) prove statements about code or specifications of real implementations; they require expertise and time, and I describe them here from general knowledge without having used them in this lab. In between, **model checking** explores every reachable state of a finite model of a protocol and checks a property in each.

The listing does two verifications that can be run in seconds. First, the **Montgomery** and **Barrett** reductions used in ML-KEM-style reference code: it checks, for every input in the documented range (218,169,343 values for Montgomery with |a| < q·2^15, and all 65,536 signed 16-bit values for Barrett), that the result is congruent to the right value modulo q and lies in the claimed range, and shows that a constant that is off by one passes the congruence check but fails the range check. Second, an **explicit-state model** of the downgrade of 10.9 with four binary parameters (16 states): it evaluates the safety property in every state, with and without the client policy rule. Everything here runs on your own machine against code and keys that exist only inside the lesson. Where a physical effect is involved (power leakage, injected faults) it is SIMULATED and labelled so. The reference libraries are slow pure-Python code: the lessons show how controls are built and, above all, how to test them.

import itertools
import numpy as np

q = 3329

# --- 1. verification by exhaustion of the modular-reduction routines used in ML-KEM reference-style code
QINV = pow(q, -1, 1 << 16)                                                  # q^-1 mod 2^16, as a signed 16-bit value
QINV_SIGNED = QINV - (1 << 16) if QINV >= (1 << 15) else QINV
print("q^-1 mod 2^16 =", QINV, "(signed", QINV_SIGNED, ")")

def montgomery_reduce_vec(a):
    # t = (int16)(a * QINV);  result = (a - t * q) >> 16   -- returns a * 2^-16 mod q, as a small signed value
    t = ((a * QINV_SIGNED + (1 << 15)) & 0xFFFF) - (1 << 15)               # the low 16 bits of a*QINV interpreted as signed
    return (a - t * q) >> 16

limit = q << 15                                                            # the documented input range: |a| < q * 2^15
bad_congruence = 0
worst_low, worst_high = 0, 0
total = 0
R_INV = pow(1 << 16, -1, q)
for start in range(-limit + 1, limit, 1 << 22):
    a = np.arange(start, min(start + (1 << 22), limit), dtype=np.int64)
    r = montgomery_reduce_vec(a)
    bad_congruence += int(np.count_nonzero((r - a * R_INV) % q))
    worst_low, worst_high = min(worst_low, int(r.min())), max(worst_high, int(r.max()))
    total += len(a)
print(f"Montgomery reduction checked for all {total:,} inputs with |a| < q * 2^15: congruence a * 2^-16 mod q violated {bad_congruence} times; results lie in [{worst_low}, {worst_high}] within (-q, q): {-q < worst_low and worst_high < q}")

V = ((1 << 26) + q // 2) // q                                              # the Barrett constant round(2^26 / q)
a16 = np.arange(-(1 << 15), 1 << 15, dtype=np.int64)
t = (V * a16 + (1 << 25)) >> 26
r = a16 - t * q
print(f"Barrett reduction with v = {V}: checked for all {len(a16):,} signed 16-bit inputs; congruent to a mod q in all cases: {bool(np.all((r - a16) % q == 0))}; results lie in [{int(r.min())}, {int(r.max())}] (about +/- q/2: {int(r.max()) <= (q + 1) // 2 and int(r.min()) >= -(q + 1) // 2})")
print("an exhaustive check over the input range IS a proof for that range: no sampling, no assumption beyond the stated bounds, and it fails loudly if a constant is wrong")
wrong_v = V - 1
t = (wrong_v * a16 + (1 << 25)) >> 26
r_bad = a16 - t * q
print(f"the same check with v = {wrong_v} (one off): results leave the range [-q/2, q/2]: min {int(r_bad.min())}, max {int(r_bad.max())}; the congruence still holds, so only the range check catches this bug")

# --- 2. explicit-state model checking of the downgrade scenario of lesson C10.9: enumerate EVERY combination of attacker capability, client policy and server support
def handshake(client_requires_pq, server_supports_pq, attacker_strips, attacker_breaks_classical):
    offer = ["PQ", "classical"]
    if attacker_strips:
        offer = [g for g in offer if g != "PQ"]
    chosen = "PQ" if ("PQ" in offer and server_supports_pq) else "classical"
    if client_requires_pq and chosen != "PQ":
        return "aborted"                                                   # client policy refuses classical-only key exchange
    if attacker_strips and chosen == "classical":
        # the transcript MAC is keyed from the classical secret; it detects the stripped offer only if the attacker cannot break it
        return "established with classical (forged)" if attacker_breaks_classical else "aborted"
    return "established with " + chosen

print()
print("model: every combination of the four binary parameters (16 states); property P = 'the connection is never established with the classical group while the client requires PQ'")
print(f"{'client requires PQ':>19} {'server has PQ':>14} {'attacker strips':>16} {'attacker breaks classical':>26} {'outcome':<36} {'P holds'}")
violations = 0
for cr, sp, st, br in itertools.product((False, True), repeat=4):
    outcome = handshake(cr, sp, st, br)
    holds = not (cr and outcome.endswith("classical") or cr and "classical (forged)" in outcome)
    violations += not holds
    print(f"{str(cr):>19} {str(sp):>14} {str(st):>16} {str(br):>26} {outcome:<36} {holds}")
print(f"P is violated in {violations} of 16 states")
unprotected = [(cr, sp, st, br) for cr, sp, st, br in itertools.product((False, True), repeat=4) if handshake(cr, sp, st, br).startswith("established with classical")]
print("states where a connection ends on the classical group:", len(unprotected), "| among them those with the client requiring PQ:", sum(1 for u in unprotected if u[0]))
print("the model checker finds the property holds in all 16 states of THIS model because the client policy aborts; remove the policy rule and the same enumeration exposes the attack states")
def handshake_no_policy(sp, st, br):
    return handshake(False, sp, st, br)
violating_without_policy = [(sp, st, br) for sp, st, br in itertools.product((False, True), repeat=3) if "forged" in handshake_no_policy(sp, st, br)]
print("without the policy rule, the forged-downgrade states are:", violating_without_policy, "(the attacker strips PQ AND can break the classical group)")
print("limits: a model checks the model; it says nothing about code that differs from it, about parameters left out of the model, or about attackers more capable than the ones enumerated")

blocks.markdown:
The Montgomery reduction is congruent to a·2^-16 modulo q for all 218,169,343 inputs and its outputs lie in [−3328, 3328], within (−q, q); the Barrett reduction with v = 20159 is congruent to a for all 65,536 inputs and its results lie in [−1664, 1664]. With v = 20158 the congruence still holds but the range reaches ±1665: **only the range check catches the bug**, which is a reminder that a verification checks exactly the properties it states and nothing else. The model check evaluates all 16 states: the property "the connection is never established with the classical group while the client requires post-quantum" holds in every state *because* the client policy aborts, and the enumeration without that rule finds the forged-downgrade states (the attacker strips the post-quantum group **and** can break the classical group).

**What formal methods give and what they don't.** They give certainty about a specified property of a specified model or program, replacing sampling with proof. They do not cover what is not specified (side channels, if the model does not include timing; hardware faults; the compiler's behaviour, unless the compiler is verified), and the proof is only as good as the specification: a verified implementation of the wrong specification is still wrong. They are most valuable for small, critical, well-understood components (arithmetic routines, parsers, protocol state machines) and for the security proofs of constructions; post-quantum implementations with machine-checked correctness and constant-time proofs exist in the literature, but I did not evaluate them here.

sections.title: 11.12 Security Evaluation
sections.summary: An evidence-based evaluation report that runs checks, records PASS or FAIL, and reports everything not assessed as 'No verified result available', ending in an overall verdict that cannot be better than the evidence.

blocks.markdown:
A **security evaluation** answers a question for a decision-maker: *is this component acceptable for this use?* A useful evaluation has a scope (which version, which platform, which threat model), a list of **claims** to be examined, **evidence** for each claim and a clear statement of what was **not** examined. The common failure is a report that is a list of passed tests, which reads as safe, with the untested risks missing. In Q-CAPS the rule is stricter: **if a result cannot be obtained reliably, the report says "No verified result available" and does not substitute an assumption**, and a verdict cannot be better than the weakest missing evidence.

The listing builds a small evaluation of the ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-44 reference modules of this lab. Ten checks are defined; five are executed (known-answer reproducibility, agreement with an independent implementation over 18 cross-checks, refusal of malformed inputs, implicit rejection, and detection of key corruption in four regions of a stored private key) and five are declared **NOT ASSESSED** because they need methods this evaluation did not run (constant-time of compiled code, power analysis, fault resistance on hardware, entropy-source assessment, supply-chain provenance). The report is printed as a table and as a machine-readable record, followed by the overall verdict. Everything here runs on your own machine against code and keys that exist only inside the lesson. Where a physical effect is involved (power leakage, injected faults) it is SIMULATED and labelled so. The reference libraries are slow pure-Python code: the lessons show how controls are built and, above all, how to test them.

import hashlib, hmac, json, random
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import mlkem, mldsa
from kyber_py.ml_kem import ML_KEM_768
from dilithium_py.ml_dsa import ML_DSA_44

# A security evaluation reports EVIDENCE, and says plainly what has not been assessed. Statuses: PASS (evidence produced here), FAIL, NOT ASSESSED (no verified result available).
rng = random.Random(1112)
kem = ML_KEM_768

def check_known_answer():
    def run():
        h = hashlib.sha256()
        for i in range(5):
            ek, dk = kem.key_derive(hashlib.shake_256(b"seed%d" % i).digest(64))
            key, ct = kem._encaps_internal(ek, hashlib.shake_256(b"m%d" % i).digest(32))
            h.update(ek + dk + ct + key)
        return h.hexdigest()
    return run() == run(), "fingerprint reproducible over 5 fixed-seed runs"
def check_cross_implementation():
    ok = 0
    for _ in range(15):
        seed = bytes(rng.getrandbits(8) for _ in range(64))
        ek, dk = kem.key_derive(seed)
        key, ct = kem.encaps(ek)
        ok += mlkem.MLKEM768PrivateKey.from_seed_bytes(seed).decapsulate(ct) == key
    dsa = ML_DSA_44
    for _ in range(3):
        seed = bytes(rng.getrandbits(8) for _ in range(32))
        pk, sk = dsa.key_derive(seed)
        sig = mldsa.MLDSA44PrivateKey.from_seed_bytes(seed).sign(b"m")
        ok += dsa.verify(pk, b"m", sig)
    return ok == 18, f"{ok} of 18 cross-checks agree with OpenSSL"
def check_input_validation():
    ek, dk = kem.keygen(); key, ct = kem.encaps(ek)
    def refused(fn):
        try: fn(); return False
        except ValueError: return True
    results = [refused(lambda: kem.encaps(ek[:-1])), refused(lambda: kem.decaps(dk, ct[:-1])), refused(lambda: kem.decaps(dk[:-1], ct))]
    return all(results), f"{sum(results)} of 3 malformed inputs refused"
def check_implicit_rejection():
    ek, dk = kem.keygen(); key, ct = kem.encaps(ek)
    bad = bytearray(ct); bad[3] ^= 1
    out = kem.decaps(dk, bytes(bad))
    return out == hashlib.shake_256(dk[-32:] + bytes(bad)).digest(32), "tampered ciphertext returns SHAKE256(z || c)"
def check_key_integrity_coverage():
    ek, dk = kem.keygen()
    covered = 0
    for region in (range(0, 100), range(1200, 1250), range(2340, 2350), range(2380, 2400)):          # secret vector, embedded ek, H(ek), z
        pos = list(region)[0]
        bad = bytearray(dk); bad[pos] ^= 1
        try:
            kem.decaps(bytes(bad), kem.encaps(ek)[1]); detected = False
        except ValueError:
            detected = True
        covered += detected
    return False, f"built-in checks detected corruption in {covered} of 4 key regions (secret vector, embedded ek, H(ek), z); an external integrity tag is required for the rest"

CHECKS = [
    ("F1", "functional", "deterministic known-answer fingerprint", check_known_answer),
    ("F2", "interoperability", "agreement with an independent implementation", check_cross_implementation),
    ("S1", "input handling", "malformed inputs are refused", check_input_validation),
    ("S2", "protocol", "invalid ciphertexts handled by implicit rejection", check_implicit_rejection),
    ("S3", "key storage", "corruption of a stored private key is detected in every region", check_key_integrity_coverage),
    ("S4", "side channels", "timing and cache behaviour of the COMPILED code is constant-time", None),
    ("S5", "side channels", "resistance to power and electromagnetic analysis (physical device)", None),
    ("S6", "faults", "resistance to fault injection on the target hardware", None),
    ("S7", "randomness", "entropy source assessed and health tests running in the product", None),
    ("S8", "supply chain", "provenance and reproducible build of every dependency", None),
]
report = []
for cid, category, text, fn in CHECKS:
    if fn is None:
        report.append({"id": cid, "category": category, "check": text, "status": "NOT ASSESSED", "evidence": "No verified result available (needs a method this evaluation did not run)"})
    else:
        ok, evidence = fn()
        report.append({"id": cid, "category": category, "check": text, "status": "PASS" if ok else "FAIL", "evidence": evidence})

print(f"{'id':<4} {'category':<17} {'status':<13} {'check'}")
for r in report:
    print(f"{r['id']:<4} {r['category']:<17} {r['status']:<13} {r['check']}")
print()
for r in report:
    print(f"{r['id']}: {r['evidence']}")
counts = {s: sum(1 for r in report if r["status"] == s) for s in ("PASS", "FAIL", "NOT ASSESSED")}
print()
print("summary:", counts)
verdict = "CANNOT BE RATED: required evidence is missing" if counts["NOT ASSESSED"] else ("NOT ACCEPTABLE" if counts["FAIL"] else "ACCEPTABLE")
if counts["FAIL"] and not counts["NOT ASSESSED"]:
    verdict = "NOT ACCEPTABLE"
print("overall:", verdict + (f" ({counts['FAIL']} failing, {counts['NOT ASSESSED']} not assessed)" if counts["FAIL"] or counts["NOT ASSESSED"] else ""))
print("a passing functional suite is necessary and not sufficient; missing evidence is reported as missing, never filled in with an assumption")
print()
print("machine-readable form of the first record:", json.dumps(report[0]))

Four checks pass, one fails and five are not assessed. The failure is a **real finding of this lesson series**: the built-in checks of the decapsulation key detect corruption in only two of its four regions (the embedded encapsulation key and its hash), not in the secret vector or in z, so an external integrity mechanism is required (9.4). The five unassessed items are listed with the text "No verified result available (needs a method this evaluation did not run)" and the overall verdict is **CANNOT BE RATED: required evidence is missing**. That is the correct conclusion: a functional suite passing on a reference implementation says nothing about side channels, hardware faults or provenance.

**Using the pattern.** Fix the scope and the threat model first (a laptop library and a payment HSM need different evidence); require evidence for every claim, in a form someone else can rerun; keep the machine-readable record with the version and date; and treat NOT ASSESSED as a result with consequences, not as a blank. Where a standard or programme requires validation (for example module validation under a national scheme), the evaluation prepares for it and does not replace it. This closes the module: attacks (C10) mapped to controls with tests (11.1 to 11.11) and to an honest account of what remains unproven.

modules.notes: Rewrites twelve outline sections (11.1 to 11.12; the capstone and certificate sections are untouched) as lessons with executed listings: a control matrix with live tests, constant-time helpers with a bytecode-level tracer, an HMAC_DRBG with health tests, envelope encryption and Shamir sharing, simulated masking, measured fault detection, a strict sealed-message format, an agility registry, the RFC 10024 hybrid layout, a mutation fuzzer, exhaustive verification of Montgomery and Barrett reduction with a model check, and an evidence-based evaluation report.
learning_objectives: Build a control matrix that pairs each attack with a control and a test, and name what the tests cannot cover.
Write and check constant-time building blocks and explain the resolution limits of source-level trace tools.
Implement an HMAC_DRBG from the standard, test its properties, and apply continuous health tests.
Protect keys with authenticated wrapping, rotation and threshold sharing, and test the failure cases.
Apply masking and fault-detection countermeasures and measure what they achieve and what remains.
Design agile, hard-to-misuse formats and hybrid deployments, and verify them by fuzzing, exhaustive checks and model checking.
Produce an evaluation that reports missing evidence as missing.
